subject: Maths
title: Fibonacci-type sequences
subtitle: Sequences · GCSE Maths
learning_objective: I can generate and analyse Fibonacci-type sequences where each term is the sum of the two preceding terms.

key_vocab.definition: A Fibonacci-type sequence is one where each term equals the sum of the two previous terms. The classic Fibonacci sequence starts 1, 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 13, ...

sections.title: Learning Objective
sections.content: I can generate and analyse Fibonacci-type sequences where each term is the sum of the two preceding terms.

sections.title: Key Words
sections.content: Fibonacci-type sequence -- A Fibonacci-type sequence is one where each term equals the sum of the two previous terms. The classic Fibonacci sequence starts 1, 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 13, ...

sections.title: Method
sections.content:
Each term is the sum of the previous two: un = un−1 + un−2.
un = un−1 + un−2
Add the two previous terms to get the next

Key examples:
  ✓ 1, 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 13, 21, ...  (classic Fibonacci)
  ✓ 2, 5, 7, 12, 19, 31, ...  (Fibonacci-type (starts 2, 5))
  ✓ Each term = sum of previous two terms  (the rule)
  ✗ 1, 1, 2, 3, 5, 9, ...  (5 + 3 = 8, not 9)
  ✗ Fibonacci sequences always start with 1, 1  (can start with any pair)

sections.title: Worked Example
sections.content:
Example 1 – continuing a sequence
  Continue the sequence 3, 7, 10, 17, ... for two more terms.
  Next term: 10 + 17 = 27
  Then: 17 + 27 = 44
  Sequence: 3, 7, 10, 17, 27, 44
  27, 44
  (Each term is the sum of the two before it.)

Example 2 – finding a missing term
  In the sequence _, _, 5, 8, 13, find the two missing terms.
  Third term (5) = first + second
  8 = second + 5, so second = 3
  5 = first + 3, so first = 2. Sequence: 2, 3, 5, 8, 13
  2, 3
  (Work backwards by subtracting: previous = current − the one before.)

sections.title: Problem solving
sections.content:
Answer each question.

(a) 8th Fibonacci number (start 1, 1)?
(b) Sum of first 8 Fibonacci numbers?
(c) Start a, b: 3rd term? 5th term?
(d) If 3rd term is 10 and 5th is 23, find 4th term.
(e) Ratio of consecutive Fibonacci numbers approaches...?

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
✓ In a Fibonacci-type sequence, each term is the sum of the previous two
✗ All Fibonacci-type sequences must start with 1, 1
✓ To find a previous term, subtract: un−2 = un − un−1
✗ Fibonacci sequences always increase
✓ The ratio of consecutive Fibonacci numbers approaches the golden ratio

teacher_sections.content:
Award marks for correct working and final answers.

Continuing sequences:
  (a) 13, 21
  (b) 21, 34
  (c) 23, 37
  (d) 34, 55

Different starting values:
  (a) 1, 3, 4, 7, 11, 18
  (b) 2, 5, 7, 12, 19, 31
  (c) 4, 4, 8, 12, 20, 32
  (d) 1, 10, 11, 21, 32, 53

Finding missing terms:
  (a) First two: 2, 1 (since 1+2=3... wait: ?, ?, 3, 5 so ?+?=3 and ?+3=5 gives ?=2, first=1)
  (b) 4, 3
  (c) ?, 4, 6, 10; first = 2 (since 2+4=6)... answer: 2, then 6
  (d) 5, 8 (since 5+8=13), middle=8; sequence: 5, 8, 13

With negative numbers:
  (a) −1, 2, 1, 3, 4, 7
  (b) 3, −2, 1, −1, 0, −1
  (c) −3, −2, −5, −7, −12, −19
  (d) 0, 1, 1, 2, 3, 5

Problem solving:
  (a) 21
  (b) 33 (actually: 1+1+2+3+5+8+13+21=54)
  (c) a+b; a+3b... (3rd=a+b, 4th=a+2b, 5th=2a+3b)
  (d) 13 (since 4th = 5th − 3rd = 23 − 10 = 13)
  (e) The golden ratio φ ≈ 1.618
